lesson.title: A President's Parting Warning to the Nation He Built
lesson.summary: Published as a letter in September 1796, Washington's Farewell Address warned against political parties, permanent foreign alliances, and sectionalism, while his voluntary retirement set the precedent of a two term presidency.
lesson.body:
As his second term wound down in 1796, George Washington chose not to seek a third, a decision with no constitutional requirement behind it since the original Constitution set no limit on presidential terms. Rather than deliver his farewell as a speech, Washington published it as a letter, first appearing in Philadelphia's American Daily Advertiser on September 19, 1796, so that it could be read and reread across the country. He worked on the document for years, drawing on an earlier draft Madison had prepared back in 1792 when Washington first considered retiring, and turning in his final years to Hamilton for extensive help polishing the language.

The address reflected lessons Washington had drawn from eight years of watching the young republic nearly tear itself apart, first over Hamilton's financial program and the national bank, then over how to respond to the French Revolution and the war between France and Britain. Washington devoted much of the letter to warning against the rise of political parties, which he worried would place loyalty to faction above loyalty to country and could be exploited by ambitious men or foreign powers to divide Americans against one another, exactly the kind of split he had watched grow between Jefferson and Hamilton inside his own cabinet.

He also warned against permanent alliances with foreign nations, urging Americans to extend commercial relations abroad while avoiding political entanglements that might drag the young and still militarily weak country into European wars. This advice grew directly out of the crisis touched off by the French Revolution, when Jefferson had favored supporting revolutionary France and Hamilton had pushed for closer ties with Britain, a split Washington had tried to resolve with his Neutrality Proclamation of 1793. Washington was not counseling permanent isolation so much as urging the country to build up its own strength before committing to fights that were not its own.

A third major theme was sectionalism, the danger that regional loyalties, north versus south or east versus the growing west, could pull the union apart before it had time to mature. Washington argued that the shared benefits of union, in trade, defense, and prosperity, far outweighed whatever narrow advantages any single region might gain from going its own way. Coming from the man who had led the Continental Army and presided over the Constitutional Convention, this appeal carried enormous moral weight.

Perhaps the address's most lasting practical legacy was simpler than any of its arguments, by voluntarily stepping down after two terms, Washington set an unwritten precedent that no president broke until Franklin Roosevelt ran for a third term in 1940, a norm later written into law by the Twenty Second Amendment in 1951. His retirement also opened the way for the presidential election of 1796 and beyond, contests that would soon test his warnings about party spirit as Federalists and Democratic-Republicans fought openly for the first time over who would lead the country he had done so much to establish.
